scores.evidence: Scheduling apps make many small database calls, and the network delay between sites hurts performance.
scores.rationale: Replication options (Always On/distributed AGs, Data Guard, logical replication, DMS), queue-pause semantics, latency effects of split tiers, and single-writer cutover mechanics are all stated accurately, including real vendor-support limits.

scores.evidence: Users should see at most a few seconds of slowness, not an outage.
scores.rationale: Directly solves zero-downtime migration with a realistic lift-and-shift, interprets the ambiguity honestly, states what it cannot know, and offers a lower-risk phased alternative.

scores.evidence: One switch point: put a load balancer or proxy in front of the app, and a stable DNS name or connection endpoint in front of the database
scores.rationale: The single-writer principle is honored consistently from core idea through cutover sequence, rollback and the phased alternative, with clear data ownership at every phase.

scores.evidence: Go/no-go criteria are met: replication lag under a few seconds, reconciliation clean, rehearsals passed.
scores.rationale: Validation targets the actual risks (lag, reconciliation checksums, shadow reads, load at measured peak, zone/network failure tests, twice-rehearsed rollback) with checkable criteria before commitment and hypercare after.

scores.evidence: I don't know your vendor, database, cloud provider or integrations, so this plan is written to work across most setups.
scores.rationale: Unknowns are declared upfront, estimates are labeled as rough and conditional, and the closing questions identify exactly which assumptions would change the plan.

scores.evidence: Messages lost during the switch | Pause and queue at the interface engine, then reconcile message counts
scores.rationale: Double-booking, lost HL7 messages, missed integrations, link failure and vendor refusal all get concrete handling, but duplicate messages on queue resume, backup/restore from corruption and security-abuse failures are thin.

scores.evidence: Hypercare: help desk staff on site with users, daily check-ins, and close watching of performance, interface errors and replication.
scores.rationale: Cutover operations, IaC, monitoring signals and command-center roles are concrete, but steady-state incident ownership, alerting, backup/restore operations and access administration after hypercare are not addressed.

scores.evidence: confirm the vendor supports your target cloud setup and licensing
scores.rationale: Beyond a licensing check and a rough timeline, cloud run costs, Direct Connect, dual-running costs during replication and people costs are ignored.

scores.evidence: Keep on-prem warm with reverse replication for 2–4 weeks as a rollback option.
scores.rationale: Effort is concentrated on the one-way decision (cutover) with explicit, rehearsed exit paths, deferred decommissioning, and the interface-engine placement flagged as a decision with trade-offs.

scores.evidence: This lowers risk but adds complexity, because every location needs one clear system of record at any given moment.
scores.rationale: Pure lift-and-shift with no re-architecting; every component (proxy, replication, hybrid link, IaC) earns its place and added complexity is explicitly weighed.

scores.evidence: Pause the interface engine's outbound queues. Messages build up safely instead of being lost.
scores.rationale: Phased ordering with dependencies, a numbered second-by-second cutover sequence, measurable gate criteria and rollback triggers let a team start immediately, with remaining specifics tied to stated unknowns.

checklist.evidence: Business Associate Agreement (BAA) signed with the cloud provider... encryption in transit and at rest, customer-managed keys, audit logging, access controls
Integrations are where scheduling migrations usually fail. List every connection... Pause the interface engine's outbound queues... Point the load balancer, DNS and interface endpoints
first full copy of the data, then keep it in sync continuously... Daily reconciliation: compare row counts and checksums... next 90 days of appointments match exactly
never let two systems accept bookings at the same time... Put the on-prem app into read-only mode, or hold new connections at the proxy
Rehearse cutover and rollback at least twice... set up reverse replication back to on-prem so you can roll back
a dedicated private link to the cloud (AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute or GCP Interconnect) with a site-to-site VPN as backup
maximum acceptable data loss and recovery time (RPO/RTO)... spread over at least two zones... printed or exported schedules for the next 72 hours
Internal | Call center/phone system, reporting/data warehouse, single sign-on
Shadow traffic: replay real read and search traffic against the cloud copy... Load test at 1.5–2× your measured peak
lowest-volume period, such as early Sunday morning... change freeze around cutover... A command center is staffed... Hypercare: help desk staff on site
confirm the vendor supports your target cloud setup and licensing... final archive, data retention per policy, certified media destruction

traps.evidence: Copy data to the cloud continuously while the on-prem system stays in charge. Then switch... in one quick, rehearsed step that you can undo.
Only one system accepts bookings at any moment; never write to both
Business Associate Agreement (BAA) signed with the cloud provider (HIPAA in the US...). Use only services the BAA covers.
Inbound feeds | ADT (patient admit/transfer feeds)... HL7 SIU messages (appointment updates) to the EHR, billing/eligibility
Keep the app and its database together.

note: An exemplary zero-downtime migration plan—single-writer discipline, CDC with reconciliation, rehearsed reversible cutover—weak only on cost realism, identity/break-glass, and tested backups.
